items.title: Mass spectrometry can tell apart molecules differing by less than a proton's mass
items.claim: A high-resolution mass spectrometer can distinguish CO (28.0101 u) from N2 (28.0061 u) — molecules differing by 0.004 mass units. Modern instruments achieve resolutions of 1 part in 100,000 or better.
items.prompt: How does that level of resolution work in practice?

options.text: By using a more sensitive scale

By measuring the frequency of ion oscillation in an electromagnetic field (Fourier-transform ion-cyclotron-resonance or Orbitrap); ion frequency is a precise function of mass-to-charge, and modern electronics measure frequencies to extraordinary precision
By averaging millions of low-resolution scans

items.reveal:
In an FTMS, ions trapped in a magnetic field orbit at a frequency f = qB / (2 pi m). Detecting their image current and Fourier-transforming gives the mass to 1 part in 10 to the 6 or better.

This is why mass spectrometry can identify peptides by their exact mass alone, or distinguish isotope clusters in metabolites. Proteomics, drug metabolism studies, environmental analysis and forensics depend on it.

The difference between CO and N2 (0.004 u) comes from the slightly different defects of binding energy in the two nuclei. Mass spec can probe nuclear physics through everyday chemistry samples.
items.why: Mass spectrometry sounds like 'a scale for molecules'. It's really a precision frequency measurement of trapped ions in fields.

items.title: Strong and concentrated are completely different
items.claim: A 0.0001 M solution of hydrochloric acid is a strong acid but dilute. A 12 M solution of ethanoic acid is concentrated but weak. Strength and concentration are independent properties of an acid.
items.prompt: What does 'strong' actually mean for an acid?

options.text: It feels acidic on the tongue
It is fully dissociated into ions in water (Ka very large); concentration is just how much acid is dissolved per unit volume
It is sold in glass bottles

items.reveal:
Strong acids — HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4 — dissociate essentially 100 percent in water. [H+] equals the acid concentration.

Weak acids — CH3COOH, HCN, H2CO3, HF — only partially dissociate. Vinegar is about 1 M ethanoic acid but [H+] is only about 0.004 M; most molecules stay intact.

Very dilute HCl is still strong (fully dissociated) but has a low [H+] and a high pH near 7. Glacial ethanoic acid is very concentrated but most molecules are undissociated — pH only modestly below 7 until water is added.

pKa describes strength; molarity describes concentration. They are independent properties.
items.why: Strength and concentration are routinely conflated. They measure entirely different physical properties of an acid.

items.title: Pure water dissolves more silver chloride than salt water does
items.claim: Silver chloride is famously insoluble — Ksp is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10. But it dissolves slightly. Try to dissolve it in salt water and the solubility plummets to almost zero.
items.prompt: Why does adding more Cl- decrease AgCl solubility?

options.text: Le Chatelier — adding more Cl- shifts AgCl(s) is in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- back to the left, reducing dissolved Ag+ until [Ag+][Cl-] equals Ksp again
Silver chloride decomposes in salt water
Salt water becomes saturated with itself, leaving no room for AgCl

items.reveal:
Suppose in pure water solubility 's' equals square root of Ksp, around 1.3 times 10 to the minus 5 M for AgCl.

In 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl-] is dominated by the salt (about 0.1 M). [Ag+] must satisfy [Ag+] times 0.1 equals 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10, so [Ag+] is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 9 M. Solubility drops by a factor of nearly 10,000.

This is exploited in gravimetric analysis: precipitate the analyte by adding excess of a common ion, ensuring almost everything comes out of solution.
items.why: Students think 'dissolved + dissolved = more dissolved'. Le Chatelier flips the intuition for ionic equilibria.
